papers.title: Role of Watch Section Task Analysis in the Development of Advanced Processor Builds
papers.authors: T. Roy*, K. Roncal*, et al. (*equal contribution)
papers.venue: Submarine Technology Symposium, JHU/APL — a classified symposium; proceedings are not publicly published
papers.plain: Her first published work, published under her earlier surname, Roncal. Submarine sonar systems were being upgraded faster than anyone could say whether the upgrades helped. The problem was not the sailors and not the hardware — it was that no one had built a way to measure the pair of them together. She helped write the quantitative and qualitative test measures for assessing how a watch section actually performs with a new system.

papers.title: APB Technologies to Support Multi-Mission Submarine Maritime Theater Operations
papers.authors: K. Roncal, G. Banta, et al.
papers.venue: Submarine Technology Symposium, JHU/APL — a classified symposium; proceedings are not publicly published
papers.plain: The programme-level companion to the 2008 paper. By now she was assistant programme manager for Advanced Processor Build and mentoring a team of ten analysts. The recurring job: introduce Operator Machine Interfaces into the Navy’s development process, so that a new capability had to prove itself against the operator who would use it, not just on a bench.

papers.storyTitle: The same method, pointed at a hospital
papers.title: Task analysis of Intensive Care Units at Johns Hopkins (project)
papers.authors: K. Gray-Roncal, as human factors engineer, JHU/APL
papers.venue: JHU/APL project; described in her CV
papers.plain: The hinge. She took the submarine methodology — watch the operators, map the task, find where the technology and the people fail to meet — and pointed it at an intensive care unit. The work led to a mockup ICU built to inform design across multiple stakeholders and machine interfaces. Eight years before medical school, the instrument had already moved into a hospital.

papers.title: Pressure Ulcer Solutions Project: medical literature review and a medical lexicon guide for non-clinical staff
papers.venue: JHU/APL project; described in her CV
papers.plain: Systems engineers were being asked to solve bedsores, a problem that kills people in hospitals, and could not read the literature. Her deliverable was a lexicon — a translation layer between engineering and medicine. It is the most literal possible statement of what her whole career does: build the interface between two systems that cannot yet hear each other.

papers.title: Risk of gonadal failure in pediatric blood cancer patients: An intervention for reproductive success in survivors
papers.authors: L. Antognoli, N. Apseloff, J. Lu, K. Roncal (equal contribution)
papers.venue: Current Opinions in Sexual Development and Reproduction, Georgetown University Medical Center, 7(M1)
papers.plain: Written as a medical student. A review of fertility loss in children treated for blood cancer. This is the publication that fits the theory least well, and we say so plainly rather than bending it: you can call late effects an unmeasured outcome, but that is a stretch.

papers.title: Machine Intelligence from Cortical Networks (MICrONS): Human–Machine Baseline Task Lead
papers.venue: IARPA MICrONS programme; described in her CV
papers.plain: She led the design and implementation of the paradigm for comparing human and algorithm performance inside MICrONS — a large national BRAIN Initiative programme building single-synapse maps of the brain in order to improve machine intelligence. Her job was not to build the algorithm. It was to make sure the humans it would be measured against had been measured properly.

papers.title: A framework for rigorous evaluation of human performance in human and machine learning comparison studies
papers.authors: H. P. Cowley, M. Natter, K. Gray-Roncal, R. E. Rhodes, E. C. Johnson, N. Drenkow, T. M. Shead, F. S. Chance, B. Wester, W. Gray-Roncal
papers.plain: The keystone. Machine learning papers routinely claim to beat humans without saying how many humans they tested, who they were, or how they were recruited. The paper that announced "surpassing human-level performance" on ImageNet used a single annotator. This framework sets out how to build a human baseline that means something — control for memory, language and fatigue; match the trials; run it like a psychology study, ethics review included.

papers.title: Author Correction: A framework for rigorous evaluation of human performance in human and machine learning comparison studies
papers.authors: H. P. Cowley, M. Natter, K. Gray-Roncal, et al.
papers.plain: A short correction re-assigning one citation and adding a second example of a well-executed comparison. Included here because a paper about doing evaluation rigorously, which then publicly fixes its own citation, is being consistent rather than embarrassed.

papers.storyTitle: Which scan, and who pays for it
papers.title: An Algorithm to Predict New Magnetic Resonance Imaging Lesions to Support Improved Disease Surveillance in Multiple Sclerosis
papers.authors: M. S. Robinette, K. Gray-Roncal, K. C. Fitzgerald, K. Ferryman, C. Overby Taylor, J. Scott, E. S. Sotirchos, P. A. Calabresi, E. M. Mowry, W. R. Gray-Roncal
papers.venue: medRxiv preprint (v1 June 2024; v3 March 2026); presented at ANA 2024
papers.plain: Both halves of her training in one author list. MS monitoring means repeated MRI on a schedule nobody has individualised, which is expensive and burdensome. Using 1,131 patients from the Johns Hopkins MS Center, the model predicts who will show a new lesion on their next scan — AUC 0.80, sensitivity 0.72, specificity 0.75 at a deliberately sensitivity-favouring threshold. It identified 772 people who could safely wait longer. Note the asymmetry she chose: the threshold is tuned to avoid missing lesions, not to look accurate.

papers.storyTitle: A blood test for damage you cannot see yet
papers.title: Association of serum neurofilament light chain deviation levels to new lesions on magnetic resonance imaging in people with multiple sclerosis
papers.authors: K. M. Gray-Roncal, K. C. Fitzgerald, S. C. Cassard, E. M. Mowry
papers.venue: Consortium of MS Centers Annual Meeting 2025; American Neurological Association 2025
papers.plain: Neurofilament light chain is a protein that leaks into the blood when nerve fibres are damaged. The question is whether a deviation in someone’s own baseline level flags new lesions before the scan does — swapping an expensive scheduled instrument for a cheap frequent one. Same move as the phone call, at the molecular scale.

papers.title: US-based African Americans with multiple sclerosis have greater disability and lower socio-economic status than Caucasian Americans
papers.authors: K. Gray-Roncal, K. C. Fitzgerald, L. Zhovtis-Ryerson, L. Charvet, R. Naismith, P. Calabresi, E. M. Mowry
papers.venue: American Neurological Association 2018; ECTRIMS 2018; JHU Neurology & Neurosurgery Research Retreat 2018
papers.plain: Presented while she was still a medical student, three years before the journal paper. Her CV records that during this period she was simultaneously "providing engineering support for upcoming technology-based clinical research studies" in the same department — a medical student who was also the department’s engineer.

papers.storyTitle: Getting a symptom into a database
papers.title: Acceptability and Usage of the PROSe Mobile System Among Pediatric Patients with Chronic Headache: A Pilot Study
papers.authors: K. Gray-Roncal, E. S. Probasco, C. Oakley, R. J. Steele, W. Stewart, M. Baker, J. Pinelis, N. Horton, A. Stanfield, H. A. Puttgen, S. Swetz, J. Probasco
papers.plain: The migraine app she had project-managed in 2015, tested on children with chronic headache. She led its design through a think-tank that put human factors engineers, graphic artists, neurologists and an actual migraine patient in one room. The outcome measured here is not headache — it is whether patients will use the instrument at all. An instrument nobody uses records nothing.

papers.storyTitle: The gap that survived the explanation
papers.title: Association of Disease Severity and Socioeconomic Status in Black and White Americans With Multiple Sclerosis
papers.authors: K. Gray-Roncal, K. C. Fitzgerald, L. Zhovtis Ryerson, L. Charvet, S. D. Cassard, R. Naismith, D. Ontaneda, K. Mahajan, W. Castro-Borrero, E. M. Mowry
papers.plain: Her most-cited work. Across 8,744 people with MS, Black Americans had worse disability, worse scores on every objective test, more lesion volume and less grey matter than White Americans — after adjusting for education, employment and insurance. The paper then does something rarer: it reports that lower neighbourhood socioeconomic status tracked worse scores among White Americans, but that this association was much less clear among Black Americans. Money did not buy the same outcome.

papers.title: POMS: A Clinical View — pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis
papers.authors: H. Chen, K. Gray-Roncal (her CV records equal contribution)
papers.venue: eMultipleSclerosis Review 6(2), CME issue and podcast, 15 September 2024
papers.plain: A clinical education review on children with MS, where the detection problem is at its worst: symptoms get attributed to something else, diagnosis is late, and treatment decisions are made on thin evidence. The through-line is identification — the same word, one more time.

papers.title: Increased contact with clinical trial participants may improve confirmed multiple sclerosis relapse detection
papers.authors: K. Gray-Roncal, M. J. Appiah, K. Zorn, K. C. Smith, S. D. Cassard, K. Fitzgerald, E. M. Mowry
papers.plain: First author, and the cleanest statement of the whole method. In the VIDAMS vitamin D trial, coordinators contacted participants between visits and asked specific questions about symptoms. The odds of a confirmed relapse being detected in the two weeks after that contact, versus the two weeks before, were 2.93 times higher. The relapses were always there. The asking is what changed.

papers.storyTitle: Building the instrument that did not exist
papers.title: Identifying racist microaggressions in health system encounters with people participating in neurology care and research
papers.authors: K. M. Gray-Roncal, S. Freeman, E. M. Mowry
papers.plain: The end of the ladder. Her 2021 paper concluded that the disparity survived every socioeconomic explanation it could measure, and pointed at "other societal constructs (e.g., systemic racism)" as the place to look next. The obvious objection is that you cannot measure that. This is her going and building the instrument. The verb in the title is identifying.

papers.title: The College Prep Program at APL: An Experiential Model to Help High-Achieving, Underserved Students Trailblaze and Achieve Success
papers.authors: K. Gray-Roncal, L. Huynh, T. Kolarik, M. Roncal, M. A. Saunders, W. Gray-Roncal
papers.venue: IEEE Integrated STEM Education Conference (ISEC) 2018, pp. 90–97
papers.plain: She co-founded this all-volunteer summer programme in 2009 and ran it for eleven years. Its premise is a measurement claim: there exist students with the desire and the academic potential to excel who will not be identified by the instruments that select for college, because those instruments are also measuring mentoring and resources. Over 220 students mentored; nearly all on track to a degree.

papers.title: An Accessible, Distributed, Technology-Based Approach for Student and Mentor Engagement
papers.authors: L. Huynh, K. Gray-Roncal, M. Roncal, W. Gray-Roncal
papers.venue: IEEE Integrated STEM Education Conference (ISEC) 2019, pp. 142–148
papers.plain: The scaling problem for the College Prep model: mentorship works, and mentorship does not travel. A technology-based approach to keeping students and mentors engaged across distance — the operator-machine interface applied to the one relationship that had been assumed to require a room.

papers.title: Toward a Framework for Providing Equitable Opportunities to Activate STEM Talent
papers.authors: S. Floryanzia, A. Jayabharathi, K. A. Carr, K. Gray-Roncal, W. Gray-Roncal
papers.venue: IEEE ISEC 2024, pp. 1–4; open version OSF Preprints (CC BY 4.0)
papers.plain: Fifteen years of running the programme, written up as a framework. The word that matters is activate: the talent is modelled as already present and unexpressed, and the thing being designed is the opportunity that would reveal it. That is the same sentence as her 2022 machine learning paper, addressed to a different population.

related.title: Performance vs. competence in human–machine comparisons
related.note: The framework her 2022 paper builds on directly. Firestone argues you must "limit machines like humans", "limit humans like machines", and align the task across species. Cowley et al. set out to operationalise the last two.

related.title: Delving deep into rectifiers: Surpassing human-level performance on ImageNet classification
related.authors: K. He, X. Zhang, S. Ren, J. Sun
related.note: The cautionary example. A paper whose title claims to surpass human-level performance, resting that claim on one human annotator with no stated evaluation method. Cited twice in her paper, under two different reference numbers.

related.title: Development of NASA-TLX (Task Load Index): Results of empirical and theoretical research
related.authors: S. G. Hart, L. E. Staveland
related.note: The workload instrument used in the 2022 study to check the task was hard enough to engage participants but not so hard as to confound them. It is a human-factors tool from aviation — the discipline she trained in — doing duty in a machine learning paper.

related.title: Brain morphology in older African Americans, Caribbean Hispanics, and Whites from Northern Manhattan
related.authors: A. M. Brickman, N. Schupf, J. J. Manly, et al.
related.note: The reference that makes the 2021 finding bite. In healthy cohorts, Black Americans have greater brain volumes than White Americans. In MS the relationship reverses — so the deficit she measures is not a baseline difference.

related.title: Neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage and 30-day rehospitalizations
related.authors: A. Kind, S. Jencks, J. Brock, et al.
related.note: The composite index of 17 socioeconomic measures she used, via 9-digit ZIP codes, to reach neighbourhood-level deprivation — a deliberately harder instrument than asking someone their income.

related.title: Multiple Sclerosis Performance Test: validation of self-administered neuroperformance modules
related.authors: S. M. Rao, R. Galioto, M. Sokolowski, et al.
related.note: The iPad instrument that produced the walking, dexterity and processing-speed numbers in her 2021 paper. A tablet that a patient operates with minimal help from staff — an operator-machine interface, in a clinic.

related.title: Effect of health care providers’ focused discussion and proactive education about relapse management on patient reporting of multiple sclerosis relapse
related.authors: R. W. Waltrip, N. Mahler, A. Ahsan, L. B. Herbert
related.note: The direct predecessor to her relapse paper: proactive provider discussion increases patient reporting. Her contribution is to run the same idea inside a randomised trial, where confirmation required a blinded neurologist rather than a patient’s account.

related.title: High-dose vitamin D3 supplementation in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: a randomised clinical trial
related.authors: S. D. Cassard, K. C. Fitzgerald, P. Qian, et al.
related.note: The parent trial: 172 randomised, 165 analysed, 96 weeks, 16 US sites. Its between-visit contacts — phone or email, checking adherence and screening for relapse symptoms — are the exposure her 2026 paper analyses.

related.title: Harnessing real-world data to inform decision-making: Multiple Sclerosis Partners Advancing Technology and Health Solutions
related.authors: E. M. Mowry, R. A. Bermel, J. R. Williams, et al.
related.note: The cohort behind the 2021 paper: standardised measurements captured during ordinary clinic visits rather than research visits, across ten MS centres. Instrumenting the encounter that was already happening.

related.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria
related.authors: X. Montalban, C. Lebrun-Frénay, J. Oh, et al.
related.note: Her 2021 paper is cited in the diagnostic criteria for the disease itself — the document that defines how dissemination in space and time is established.

related.title: Embodiment of structural racism and multiple sclerosis risk and outcomes in the USA
related.authors: A. M. Langer-Gould, T. Cepon-Robins, J. Benn Torres, et al.
related.note: The direct uptake of her closing sentence. Her paper said the residual points beyond socioeconomic status toward systemic racism; this is the field taking that up as a research programme.

related.title: Differential diagnosis of suspected multiple sclerosis: considerations in people from minority ethnic and racial backgrounds
related.authors: L. Amezcua, D. Rotstein, A. Shirani, et al.
related.note: Cites the 2021 paper in the course of rewriting how clinicians should approach diagnosis in minoritised patients — measurement feeding back into practice.

related.title: Association of Social Determinants of Health With Brain MRI Outcomes in Individuals With Pediatric Onset Multiple Sclerosis
related.authors: R. Ross, K. A. O’Neill, R. A. Betensky, et al.
related.note: Her method — social determinants against quantitative MRI outcomes — applied to children, by another group. She is not an author; the citation is the inheritance.

related.title: STREAM (ChemBio): A Standard for Transparently Reporting Evaluations in AI Model Reports
related.authors: T. McCaslin, J. Alaga, S. Nedungadi, S. Donoughe
related.note: The most surprising downstream use: her human-baseline framework being pulled into standards for how frontier AI model evaluations should be reported. A submarine human-factors lineage arriving at AI safety.

related.title: Advancing Care and Outcomes for African American Patients With Multiple Sclerosis
related.authors: A. Okai, A. M. Howard, M. Williams, et al.
related.note: A clinical-practice response in the same journal, one year later.

related.title: Perception without preconception: comparison between the human and machine learner in recognition of tissues from histological sections
related.authors: S. Barui, P. Sanyal, K. S. Rajmohan, A. Malik
related.note: A pathology group using the framework to compare human and machine tissue recognition — the intended use, in a clinical domain.

keywords.label: ascertainment
keywords.title: Ascertainment — nothing is recorded unless somebody acts
keywords.note: The idea connecting a randomised trial, a headache app and a study of racist microaggressions. In each, the outcome only enters the record if a person decides to report it, and that decision is not evenly distributed. Her fix is always the same: schedule the asking, and make the questions specific.

keywords.label: the human baseline
keywords.title: The human baseline — measure the person properly before you judge them
keywords.note: Submarine watch standers in 2008, MTurk participants in 2022, and MS patients on an iPad in 2021 are all being scored on a task. In every case her contribution is to the scoring instrument, not to the performer. This is the single strongest structural link between the defence work and the medicine.

keywords.label: the adjusted residual
keywords.title: The adjusted residual — control for the explanation you already believe
keywords.note: In the 2022 framework: control for memory, language and prior experience, then whatever difference is left is really about the algorithm. In the 2021 paper: control for education, employment, insurance and neighbourhood, then whatever gap is left is really about something else. Identical logic, ten years and two disciplines apart.

keywords.label: operator–machine interface
keywords.title: The operator–machine interface — her actual job title, twice
keywords.note: Her CV says she "led the introduction of Operator Machine Interfaces into the Navy’s advanced development process." A sonar console, an ICU, a tablet-based disability test, a migraine app and an MRI protocol are all interfaces where a person and a machine meet and one of them gets scored. She never changed jobs; the console did.

keywords.label: who is in the room
keywords.title: Who is in the room — and who the instrument was never built for
keywords.note: The bridge between the education work and the disparities work, which share no reference list at all. A college-selection process and a clinical outcome measure are both instruments that were calibrated on a population, and both mis-read people outside it. "Activate STEM talent" and "identify racist microaggressions" are the same sentence pointed at different rooms.
